notes: gigas, gigantis, m.: a Greek noun taken into the third declension, genitive plural gigantum
cor, cordis, n.: i-stem, genitive plural cordium, neuter plural corda; the stem cord- shows only from the genitive on
finis, finis, m.: i-stem, genitive plural finium; in the plural fines also means borders and territory
summitas: genitive plural summitatum
cogitatio: genitive plural cogitationum
longitudo, latitudo and altitudo all make their genitive plural in -inum (longitudinum)
bitumen: genitive plural bituminum, neuter plural bitumina
fœdus, fœderis, n.: genitive plural fœderum, neuter plural fœdera; it is a homograph of the adjective fœdus, fœda, fœdum (foul)
latus, lateris, n. (side) is a different word from latus, lata, latum (broad) and from latus, the perfect participle of fero; genitive plural laterum, neuter plural latera
sexus, sexus, m.: fourth declension, and the genitive singular sexus is identical to the nominative
sæculum, sæculi, n.: also spelt seculum; a sæculo means 'of old'
cubitus, cubiti, m.: the measure; the plural is also written cubita as a neuter
tristegum, tristegi, n.: a Greek loan for a third storey, and it occurs only in the plural here
cœnaculum, cœnaculi, n.: an upper room, from cœna (dinner), and always the room upstairs
mansiuncula, mansiunculæ, f.: the diminutive of mansio, so 'a little dwelling'
tres, tria: declines only in the plural — tres, trium, tribus, tres, tribus, with the neuter tria for the nominative and accusative
bini, binæ, bina: a distributive numeral, plural only, meaning 'two apiece'
centum, viginti, triginta and quinquaginta are indeclinable; trecenti, trecentæ, trecenta declines like the plural of bonus
potens, potentis: a one-termination third-declension adjective, and it is the present participle of possum used as an adjective
perfectus, perfecta, perfectum is the perfect participle of perficio hardened into an adjective; the participle proper is in Genesis 2 (perfecti sunt)
universus, universa, universum: unus + versus, 'turned into one', so the singular means 'the whole' and the plural 'all'
cœpi, cœpisse: defective — perfect, pluperfect and future perfect only, with no present system at all
inquam: defective — a handful of forms only, and inquit is always parenthetical inside the quotation it reports

pœnitet, pœnitere, pœnituit: impersonal — pœnitet, pœnituit and pœnitebit occur, pœniteo and pœnites never, so a personal second-conjugation citation would generate a paradigm of forms the text does not use; it takes the accusative of the person who repents (pœnituit eum, pœnitet me) and a genitive or an infinitive for the thing repented of
tollo, tollere, sustuli, sublatus: three unrelated stems, and the perfect sustuli is borrowed from suffero
mando, mandere, mandi, mansus (to chew) is a different verb from mando, mandare, mandavi, mandatus (to entrust); mandi is the passive infinitive of the first and the perfect of it as well
venit is both the present and the perfect third singular of venio; only the context and a long e separate them
disperdo, disperdere, disperdidi, disperditus: the perfect is reduplicated, like perdidi from perdo
tango, tangere, tetigi, tactus: the perfect tetigi is reduplicated and drops the n of the present stem
gigno, gignere, genui, genitus: the present is reduplicated from the root gen-, which the perfect and supine show plain
eligo, eligere, elegi, electus: a compound of lego, with the vowel weakened from leg- to lig-
corrumpo, corrumpere, corrupi, corruptus: a compound of rumpo, which loses the n of the present stem in the perfect and supine
ingredior, ingredi, ingressus sum: deponent, and the supine stem ingress- shares nothing with the present ingred-
possum, posse, potui: pot- before a vowel and pos- before s (potest but possunt); no supine at all
linio, linire, linivi, linitus: the fourth-conjugation form of lino, linere, levi, litus, which means the same thing
procreassent is syncopated for procreavissent
tecum is cum welded onto the ablative te and written backwards; the preposition follows its pronoun rather than leading it

cum is a conjunction here (cumque cœpissent, cumque vidisset) and a preposition in 6:9 and 6:13 (cum Deo, cum terra), so the preposition is cited 'cum (preposition)' to keep the two dictionary entries apart
facies is the future of facio in 6:14, 6:15 and 6:16, and the noun facies (face) in 6:7 and 6:13 — one surface form, two words
quam is the correlative adverb 'as' in 6:21, answering tam, and the relative pronoun elsewhere
hominum in 6:6 is the genitive plural governed by pœnituit, not the accusative object of fecisset; the Clementine prints hominum where many texts read hominem
